 SubjectiveCrisis.Zone — the alerts timed, the Defence Force on intercepts, the Guards on six drones, and the President’s conditionThe Interior Ministry sent threat alerts to residents on Sunday, the first such warnings since September; an agency journalist in Manama reported alarm sirens and explosions at about 4:00 a.m. local time, and residents reported a second series of blasts around 6:30 a.m. The two alerts went out at 5:32 a.m. and 7:50 a.m. Emirates time, which is 4:32 a.m. and 6:50 a.m. in Bahrain. The ministry’s posts urged citizens and residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels; it named no threat, source or target. Later that morning the Defence Force said its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets, and that Iran continues its systematic hostile approach through attacks targeting Bahraini territory, with all units at the highest level of readiness. The Guards said six of their drones targeted an American air defence radar in Bahrain; no damage or casualties had been reported, and neither American nor Bahraini authorities had confirmed any hit. The Guards’ statement, carried by the state broadcaster’s Telegram channel, by Fars and by Press TV, said the American air defense radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base was targeted by six drones of the Aerospace Force; the Guards called it the second phase of a decisive and crushing response and said the sound of the drones striking their targets was heard in several parts of Bahrain, while one account reported the statement gave no evidence of damage. On Friday the Guards said they had targeted and destroyed an early-warning radar; Central Command denied it, saying both drones were shot down with no injuries or damage. The account sets out four markers: whether Central Command confirms or denies the new claim as it did on Friday, whether Bahrain reports any damage, whether the President’s conditional pause survives a second claimed strike in three days—a wire reported Saturday that the President said he might hold off on attacking Iran if there were no new provocations from Tehran or the Houthis, while maintaining the naval blockade—and the Qatar-mediated talks, on which the President has said the United States does not need a deal.

 SubjectiveGeopolitiki — the first nationwide alert since September, six drones claimed at Al-Riffa, and no confirmation of damageBahrain sounded a nationwide alert for a possible threat in the early hours of Sunday, November 15, its first since September, while the Guards announced that six drones of their Aerospace Force hit an American air-defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base. The Guards call the attack the second phase of their retaliation for American military action against Iran. The claim of damage to the radar came without evidence and has not been confirmed by the United States or Bahrain. The Interior Ministry issued two notices, at 5:32 a.m. and 7:50 a.m. local time in the account’s reading, calling on citizens and residents to stay calm, go to the nearest safe place and get information only from official channels, without specifying the nature of the threat. Residents reported explosions around 4 a.m. and a second series at about 6:30 a.m. The Defence Force then announced that its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets. The Guards’ statement, broadcast by state television and the Tasnim agency, says the strikes were heard in various areas of Bahrain and that more drones were used in this phase than in the previous one. The first phase, in the Guards’ terminology, was the attack of Friday, November 13, when they said they destroyed an American early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for the strike at Sirik.

 SubjectiveFana News — the Foreign Ministry’s statement: Resolution 2817, Article 51, and a call on the CouncilBahrain has condemned, in the strongest terms, Iran’s continued attacks on its territory after air defence systems intercepted and destroyed drones launched on Sunday, two days after intercepting two others in a similar attack. In a statement issued on Sunday, the Foreign Ministry described the attacks as a resumption of Iran’s aggression against Bahrain and regional countries, in blatant disregard for international law and the Charter. It called them a flagrant violation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iranian attacks on Bahrain and neighboring countries and demanded their immediate cessation, while foreclosing de-escalation efforts and imperiling regional security and stability. The ministry affirmed Bahrain’s inherent individual and collective right to self-defense under Article 51 of the Charter and to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty and the security of its citizens and residents. As a member of the Security Council, Bahrain called on the Council to condemn the repeated attacks, shoulder its responsibilities, and take decisive measures to ensure Iran’s full compliance with Resolution 2817, halt its attacks and threats, and end its support for proxy groups in the region.

 SubjectiveGlobal 1 News — the intercepts, the resolution dated March 11, and Tehran’s own Article 51Bahrain’s air defences fired in anger for the first time since September, and this time the kingdom’s own military is announcing the shootdowns while the American military, which denied Tehran’s last claim two days ago, says nothing. Iran says it sent six drones at an American radar at a helicopter base outside Manama; Bahrain says it stopped the attacks. There has been no confirmation from American or Bahraini authorities that the Al-Riffa installation was struck, and one agency noted there were no claims or details of the drones having caused damage. On November 13 the Guards said they had destroyed an American early-warning radar in Bahrain, retaliation for an air attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, in Iran’s southern Hormozgan province near the Strait of Hormuz. The Foreign Ministry denounced a resumption of Iran’s aggression, said the attacks violated international law, declared that no pretext can legitimise violations of state sovereignty, and added that Bahrain rejects the use of its territory to settle accounts and holds Iran fully responsible for the attacks and their consequences. The Security Council adopted Resolution 2817 on March 11, 2026, at its 10,119th meeting, by thirteen votes to none with China and Russia abstaining; Bahrain tabled it for the Gulf Cooperation Council and it drew 135 co-sponsors. The text condemned in the strongest terms Iranian attacks against Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan, and demanded Tehran immediately and unconditionally cease provocations against its neighbours, including through proxies; Bahrain has called for it to be fully implemented, and its ambassador to the United Nations is named in the account. Tehran’s Foreign Ministry did not treat Sunday as a violation of anything: its spokesman told a news conference that attacks on Iran’s neighbours were justified under Article 51 of the Charter, which sets out a state’s right to defend itself, and he accused the Gulf states of helping Washington strike his country.

 SubjectiveSababu — Bahrain and Saudi Arabia condemn the continuing attacks, and the self-defence right restatedBahrain has strongly condemned continuing Iranian drone attacks on its territory, calling them a violation of its sovereignty and a serious threat to the security of the entire region. In a statement issued on Sunday, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the country’s air defence systems intercepted and destroyed drones launched on Sunday, as well as two drones launched last Friday. The Guards have claimed responsibility for the attacks. Bahrain said the attacks were unacceptable and a direct violation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which called on Iran to stop its attacks on Bahrain and neighbouring countries. Recalling its full right to self-defence under Article 51 of the Charter, Bahrain called on the Security Council to condemn the Iranian attacks and take decisive measures. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also strongly condemned the attacks on Bahrain.

 SubjectiveLaPresse — the Kremlin: the European negotiators have not yet contacted RussiaMilan, November 15. The negotiators appointed by the European Union have not yet attempted to contact Russia, Kremlin spokesman Peskov stated, in response to a question on the matter from the TASS agency: “No, not yet.” At the informal European summit in Dublin, the Union’s heads of state and government opted for a format that includes the European institutions and the five countries—Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland—alongside the European Commission and the Council, to represent Europe in the negotiations on Ukraine.

 SubjectiveLaPresse — the Kremlin: without an agreement with Europe, Russia will have to use forceMilan, November 15. In the absence of a negotiated solution with Europe, Russia will have to achieve its objectives by force. This is what Kremlin spokesman Peskov said in an interview with a correspondent of Vesti, according to reports from the Russian agencies. Earlier, the spokesman had told TASS that the negotiators chosen by Europe had not yet attempted to establish contact with Russia.

 SubjectiveSagire — the spokesman’s interview: no point in discussing a settlement if the Union does not want peaceKremlin spokesman Peskov said Russia will have to use force to achieve its goals if there is no prospect of reaching agreements with Europe, in an interview with a Vesti correspondent. According to the spokesman, if the European Union does not want peace, there is no point in discussing a settlement to the Ukraine conflict or the European security framework. Earlier, the spokesman had said that the negotiators chosen by Europe had not yet approached Russia.

 SubjectiveInstitute for the Study of War — the November 14 assessment: a membership proposal stated in Kyiv, a demands paper, and Europe’s inclusion arguedPresident Zelenskyy stated on November 14 that the American delegation at the November 10–11 peace talks in Abu Dhabi proposed that Ukraine gain NATO membership in exchange for a Ukrainian withdrawal from the entirety of the Donbas region. A newspaper reported on November 13 that it obtained a copy of an unofficial non-paper of demands that the Russian delegation circulated during the Abu Dhabi talks, representing Russia’s opening negotiating position, according to two sources involved in the talks; a German outlet similarly reported that Russian intermediaries presented a series of unofficial demands related to Ukraine, Europe and NATO to European representatives in Abu Dhabi. The United States continues to call for the inclusion of European delegations in upcoming multilateral negotiations: the White House’s Principal Deputy Press Secretary stated on November 13 that the American delegation at the recent trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi ensured that Europe will be included in future peace talks. A wire-service report of November 13, citing a senior European official, reported that European officials designated the national security advisers from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland and a representative of the Union to represent Europe in any future technical-level talks, and that Europe has not yet designated any European leaders to represent it. The assessment also records that the three presidents will meet at the November 18–19 APEC leaders’ meeting in China to discuss nuclear weapons proliferation and the situation in Iran, and will likely not discuss the war in Ukraine, according to the White House’s Assistant Press Secretary.

 SubjectiveCNN — the President to meet China’s and Russia’s leaders at a first trilateral sit-down on nuclear non-proliferationThe President will meet jointly next week with China’s leader and Russia’s President Putin, the White House said Friday, a first-ever trilateral sit-down between the leaders of the three countries. The meeting, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, will focus on nuclear non-proliferation, a topic the President has said he believes could yield a new agreement between the world’s biggest nuclear-armed states. The Kremlin says the meeting will take place on November 19 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, but there has been no confirmation yet from China. The last nuclear arms treaty between the United States and Russia expired in February.

 SubjectiveParticle News — the board accepts the resignation, an investigation under way, and the petition past 120,000 by SundayThe board announced Thursday that Mr. Huang resigned as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect and that the executive vice president and chief financial officer, Ms. Colette Kress, will serve as interim chief executive. An online petition called Stand with Jensen surged to more than 120,000 signatures by Sunday; it was organized by current and former employees, partners and shareholders who demand Mr. Huang be reinstated during an independent investigation. The company has confirmed an independent investigation is under way but has not disclosed its scope, independence or timeline, and the company will still release its fiscal 2027 third-quarter results on November 17 at about 1:20 p.m. Pacific with a 2:00 p.m. Pacific earnings call.

 SubjectiveTradingView, carrying Benzinga — the counter at 135,468 at 0037 on Sunday, its categories unverified, and Mr. Musk signingA petition urging the company to reinstate Mr. Huang as chief executive passed 135,000 signatures on Sunday, days after his resignation and ahead of the chipmaker’s third-quarter earnings report. The campaign site’s counter showed 135,468 signatures at 12:37 a.m. Eastern on Sunday. The site classified 6,776 signers as current employees, 1,267 as former employees and 73,181 as shareholders, though those affiliations have not been independently verified. The open letter asks the board to reinstate Mr. Huang while an independent investigation establishes the facts; it also seeks a fair hearing and a public explanation. The site says the company and Mr. Huang do not endorse it. On Friday, Tesla’s chief executive wrote on X that a petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and that he is signing it too. Mr. Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director on November 12, the company said in a press release; the chief financial officer, Ms. Colette Kress, is interim chief executive.

 SubjectiveBigGo Finance — nearly 130,000 by Saturday evening, three procedural demands, and the authenticity questionedAs of the evening of November 14, Eastern time, an online petition called Stand with Jensen had gathered nearly 130,000 signatures demanding that the board restore Mr. Huang as chief executive. The petition went live almost simultaneously with the announcement of the resignation on November 12; its organizers describe themselves as current and former employees and shareholders and state that they have no affiliation with the company. The open letter makes three requests, targeting procedural issues rather than defending Mr. Huang’s personal conduct: that he be reinstated before an independent investigation establishes the facts; that the scope, independence and timetable of the investigation be made public and that he be given a substantive opportunity to respond; and that if the board insists he must leave, it provide a specific, evidence-backed explanation. A Tesla chief executive’s post on X said he had signed the petition. The petition’s authenticity, however, has been called into question: because the website lacks real-name verification, the signatures are hard to verify, and a company vice president, Mr. Bryan Catanzaro, publicly clarified that he never signed, saying his name had been used without his consent. On November 12 the shares fell more than 14 percent intraday, briefly dropping below a $4 trillion market value before closing down 4.34 percent; measured from November 8, when the board announced the independent investigation, the stock fell 10.96 percent over four trading sessions, wiping out more than $480 billion in market value. The account also records the supply commitments in the filings and the data-center revenue shares of the last reported quarters.

 SubjectiveLanka Leader, carrying AFP — more than 100,000 rally, a decline from last week, and Tuesday’s anniversary on the roundaboutsMore than 100,000 people have taken to the streets in France in another round of cost-of-living rallies organised by the Yellow Vests and various youth movements. Saturday’s protests saw a decline in turnout compared with previous weekends and stayed largely calm, authorities said. The Interior Ministry reported that 106,000 people took part in protests nationwide, including 24,000 in Paris—down from 146,000 nationwide and 46,000 in Paris last week. The country has been gripped by high-school blockades, mass demonstrations and strikes for more than a month, with protesters rallying against falling educational standards, cost-of-living increases, low wages and police violence. Unions have called for a new day of strikes on Tuesday after rejecting a government promise to increase the minimum wage by 0.6 percent as crumbs. If the demonstrations go ahead, they will take place on the eighth anniversary of the Yellow Vest movement, which rocked the beginning of the Macron government in 2018 with two years of protests triggered by rising fuel prices. On Tuesday the Yellow Vests will celebrate their eight years where it all started: on roundabouts and toll booths all over France, a protest tracking site writes.

 SubjectiveParticle News — the fifth Saturday at 106,000, the police bill to the Senate, and a strike on TuesdayThe nationwide demonstrations ran for a fifth Saturday in a row on November 14 and the Interior Ministry put turnout at about 106,000 people, including roughly 24,000 in Paris, while organisers gave higher estimates. The movement now unites high-school students, trade unions, Yellow Vest activists and child-protection campaigners demanding better school conditions, higher pay and relief from the rising cost of living. At the centre of the protests is a bill passed by the lower house that would give officers a presumption of legitimate self-defence when they use firearms, a measure opponents call a licence to kill in the account’s words, that they say would weaken accountability. With the Senate vote pending and unions rejecting a 0.6 percent minimum-wage offer, the protests threaten to reshape law-and-order debates ahead of the 2027 presidential race, in the account’s reading, and raise the risk of further strikes and clashes next week. Senate consideration of the contested measure is set to follow union plans for a nationwide strike on Tuesday, November 17.

### No Such Thing As Monday Is the Book of the Week, Scrooge Splits the Critics in Half, and the Empress Takes Her Leave

Filed as: Sunday Review of Reviews — Weekend Features · 2026-11-15T04:10:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-15-sunday-reviews.html

Weekend Features — Sunday Review of Reviews

 Objective

 No Such Thing As Monday Is the Book of the Week, Scrooge Splits the Critics in Half, and the Empress Takes Her Leave

 The week's review lists were tallied, and the tally gave the desk a divided week. The book du jour is No Such Thing As Monday by Si&acirc;n Hughes, published in the United States on November 10: first in the week's fiction tally with five rave reviews, two positive and one mixed, taken by its reviewers to be the life of Steffie Cartwright of working-class Birmingham—a woman who finds her father dead in his chair, removes stains at a dry cleaner's, and goes looking for the sister who ran away from home at 16. On screen the week belonged to division: Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol, Ti West's telling of Dickens with Johnny Depp as Scrooge, opened November 13 with the critics split at 50 to 53 percent and the argument fixed on its leading man, while its ghosts and its design drew agreement from both camps; and The Empress, the German serial on Netflix, closed its third and final season with verdicts running from masterpiece to 3.5 of 10. A lone capsule, labeled Worth Watching, files John Wilson's documentary feature The History of Concrete. The desk states its position plainly at the head of each part: it has not read the book, and it has not watched the serial, the films, or the documentary. What follows is a review of reviews.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0410 ET, Sunday, November 15, 2026. The second Sunday Review of Reviews of this paper, filed under the Weekend Features ruling of November 4, 2026. The desk tallied the week's review lists—the New York Times Book Review and its peers, the Chicago Review of Books, the Washington reviewing tradition carried in Ron Charles's Tuesday Review, the Guardian, and the aggregating tally at Book Marks—and the week's film and television reviews, international by house rule. The clippings the report was drawn from are filed beneath it, each stamped subjective.

The Week in Brief: The Tally

In fiction, one book stood at the head of the list, and the list beneath it was crowded with clean verdicts. Book Marks' tally of the week, published November 13, ranks No Such Thing As Monday first with five rave reviews, two positive and one mixed. Behind it: Xita Rubert's The Key Biscayne Affair, three rave and two positive; Annie Proulx Stories: New & Selected, four rave and no other verdict recorded; Niall Williams's O Now!, three rave and one positive; and Gabriel Bump's Don't Stop Snowing, one rave and four positive. In nonfiction the tally's order and its arithmetic part company, and the desk prints both as filed: The Telephone: A New History by James Gleick stands first with four rave and three positive, while Nick Paumgarten's The Intangibles stands second with five rave and one positive—more raves, one place lower. Lauren Elkin's Vocal Break and Nancy Isenberg's Aristocracy, American Style share third at three rave and two positive each, and Mona Chalabi's Ten Lives closes the list at one rave and three positive.

The week's five selected single reviews point at a different shelf, and the desk files the difference. The quintet chosen this week—Hillary Kelly in The Atlantic on M. John Harrison's The End of Everything, Merve Emre in The New Yorker on Tom Overton's John Berger, Ed Park on Cleo Birdwell's Amazons, Ryan Ruby in Bookforum on Emily Ogden's Darkness Becomes Bright, and Josef Burton on Akbar Shahid Ahmed's Crossing the Red Line—contains no review of the book at the head of the tally. Last week the book du jour stood in both lists at once. This week it stands on the tally alone: eight reviews counted, seven of them favorable, from the papers and journals the tally tracks. The desk takes the tally as the week's verdict and the selected five as the week's reading, and prints the book the tally chose.

Part One — The Book: No Such Thing As Monday, by Si&acirc;n Hughes

The desk has not read this book. It says so plainly, as the house rule requires: everything in this part is what the reviewers report, agree on, and dispute, and nothing in it is the desk's reading. No Such Thing As Monday is a novel. Si&acirc;n Hughes is a British writer who began as a poet; her novel Pearl, published in 2023 and longlisted for the Booker Prize, was written in response to the medieval poem of the same name. This book was published in the United States by Henry Holt and Company on November 10, 2026: 224 pages, $26.99, ISBN 9781250459572.

On what the book is, the reviewers agree completely, and their agreement is the week's firmest fact. Stephanie Cartwright—Steffie—is a chain-smoking, prickly woman in middle age who works at a dry cleaner's in contemporary working-class England and tends to her father. The novel opens with Steffie finding that father, Stan, dead in his favorite chair. Stan dominated her childhood near Birmingham in the 1970s and 1980s: a violent bully who ran dogfights at the local pub, whose wife died before him, and whose favorite Steffie always was—a favoritism that left her carrying guilt for her older sister, Caroline, who fled home at 16 and has not been seen since. With Stan dead, Steffie sets out to find Caroline. The reviewers describe the same construction from every side: a life told in episodes across childhood to middle age, in no straight order, each chapter standing nearly on its own—in the Chicago Review of Books' account, each chapter a set of pages in a photo album, the picture widening as the album fills. And every reviewer who addresses the book's machinery names the same source under it: the medieval poem called Cleanness, or Purity, from the same 14th-century manuscript that holds Pearl and Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, which gives the novel its governing figure of the stain—the laundry Steffie cleans by day, and the past she cannot clean at all.

On what the book is taken to be, the reviewers also agree, in their own words, filed below. Leah Greenblatt of the New York Times calls it fractious and darkly funny: an ouroboros of ongoing traumas that somehow manages not to be head-smashingly bleak, because Steffie on the page is a pretty great hang—spiky, sharp-witted, blazingly self-aware—and because Hughes has a canny, lyrical ear for her misfits and underdogs, and a touch tender enough to nudge their fate toward better things. Kirkus, in its starred notice, credits an alchemy like Douglas Stuart's: Hughes transforms the dross of Steffie's life into literary gold. The Chicago Review of Books calls Steffie compelling—not always likeable, and certainly never unlikeable—and the novel a powerful story that unveils itself with every page. The Bookreporter review reaches the same resting place from the record of the plot: a profoundly sad novel, and a surprisingly hopeful one, whose message is that it is never too late to gain perspective, to make amends, or to try to start anew. The publisher's record places the book in the working-class British realist tradition of Douglas Stuart and Andrea Arnold, and the trade notices filed with it name Hughes an exceptional and compassionate chronicler of precarious and chaotic lives.

The split in the file is about the comedy, and how far it reaches into the childhood chapters. The Times of London, in the coolest review the week filed, grants the premise its full force—humour is how Steffie copes with loss, and how the reader copes with an otherwise harrowing tale of penury and hurt—and then records a falling off: as the novel dives into Steffie's violent childhood in the West Midlands, the dark comedy recedes, and Hughes could have gone further and funnier to wring the last drop of absurdity from each scene. Where the author excels, in that review's judgment, is in meandering through the slippages of memory to reveal what is gnawing at her narrator. Its verdict is measured: a decent follow-up to Pearl, even if by design it seems to position itself as the lesser work—a book that, like Steffie, cannot escape the taint of disappointment. The desk files the disagreement as it stands. Seven of the tally's eight counted verdicts are favorable, and the favorable reviews praise the humour as the book's engine; the one cool review praises the memory work and asks for more of the humour. No reviewer in the week's file faults the sentences, and no reviewer disputes Steffie herself.

Where to get it. No Such Thing As Monday by Si&acirc;n Hughes is available at Amazon. As an Amazon Associate, Objective Daily News earns from qualifying purchases made through that link.

Part Two — Screen: Scrooge, Split in Half, and the Empress Takes Her Leave

The desk has not watched any of the screen works in this part. It has not streamed The Empress, and it has not sat in a cinema for Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol or How to Rob a Bank. Their status here is the same as the book's: the reviews, reviewed.

The television pick of the week is The Empress, and it is German, and it is finished. The third and final season of the serial—Die Kaiserin in its own language, on Netflix—was released on November 12. The story it closes is the story the serial has told since 2022: Elisabeth of Austria, played by Devrim Lingnau Islamoğlu, the Bavarian duke's daughter who married Emperor Franz Joseph, played by Philip Froissant, for love and spent her reign fighting the walls of the Viennese court. The final season opens a few months after the second season's close, with Franz returned from commanding his army at the front, a changed, cold and distant man, and the imperial marriage on shaky ground; it carries the story through to the establishment of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy. On the measure that is not a review, the serial's standing is a matter of record: its first season in September 2022 became, in the reports filed below, Netflix's second-most-watched series globally on its debut, and it stands in those reports as the service's most successful German original since Barbarians.

The reviewers agree on the season's materials, and on the bargain its ending strikes. Every review in the file records a darker and more politically tangled season; every review credits the same visible strengths—the chemistry of the two leads, the costumes, in the Absolute Geeks account the work of costume designer Gabriela Reumer standing among the best in streaming period drama, and production design that no reviewer faults. And every review that reaches the ending describes the same transaction: the finale blends fiction and fact, chooses the fairytale the serial has always carried over the history book, and leaves the harrowing later record of Elisabeth's life—the loss of her son Rudolf among it—outside the frame, her assassination handled, in one account, as onscreen text before the credits. The ending turns the founding of the dual monarchy into a fresh start for the marriage, grounded in the understanding that this empress needs the freedom to be herself.

The split is about whether that bargain is the season's achievement or its evasion, and the file runs the full width of the scale. At one end, ScreenRant's November 14 account calls the third season a true masterpiece and the serial a show with no bad season, each installment better than the last. Collider calls the ending a satisfying, poignant conclusion for one of Netflix's best hidden gems, and Absolute Geeks, at four of five, calls the season a strong, confident farewell that sticks the landing where it counts—while recording, in the same review, a rushed and underdeveloped Hungarian subplot and a life-changing relationship with Count Andr&aacute;ssy given too little room. At the other end stands the Midgard Times review, at 3.5 of 10: a rushed finale that turns history into bullet points, a season that never allows any moment, scene, feeling or action to linger, speedrunning its material until investment fails—filed by a reviewer who holds that the serial peaked in a first season that was itself not all that good. Between the poles, the audience record filed on IMDb runs warm: breathtaking, heart-wrenching, viewers who waited two years and binged the season in one go. The desk files the whole width: the materials are agreed, the farewell is contested, and the contest is between a romance that has earned its ending and a history that was owed more time.

In cinemas, the week's film is Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol, and its reviewers agree on its ghosts and divide on its Scrooge. The film opened November 13, directed by Ti West and written by Nathaniel Halpern, rated PG-13 and running 116 minutes, with Johnny Depp as Scrooge in his first studio lead in eight years, Ian McKellen as Jacob Marley, Tramell Tillman, Andrea Riseborough and Daisy Ridley as the three ghosts, and Rupert Grint as Bob Cratchit. The agreement in the file is exact: the production design and the photography—Eve Stewart's design and Checco Varese's dark, fogged London, credited by name in reviews that agree on little else—and the ghost work above all, Tillman's Ghost of Christmas Present named the film's diamond in TheWrap's account and the spirits given layers, in Empire's, that outclass the picture around them. The Rotten Tomatoes consensus, as the service prints it, holds the same two facts in one sentence: evocative production design, a Depp filled with the bah-humbug spirit, and a telling that plays too safe among its long line of remakes. The division is the lead. The Daily Telegraph's Robbie Collin gave the film four of five; the Guardian's Peter Bradshaw found Depp in fact rather good; Deadline recorded a man having a blast, and The Hollywood Reporter a creepily effective comeback vehicle. Against them: the Boston Globe's Odie Henderson, at one of four, called Depp easily the worst Scrooge he had ever seen; IndieWire's David Ehrlich found him unengaging in a film named for his character; the Associated Press, at one of four, called the whole a horror-tinged holiday slog. The counts print the division without ornament: 35 fresh and 34 rotten in one count of 69, and an audience mark, when it posted, of 89 percent against the critics' half.

The week's second film is filed in one paragraph, because its split runs between the critics and the audience rather than through either camp. How to Rob a Bank, David Leitch's heist picture, opened November 13: Nicholas Hoult leads a Pittsburgh crew that livestreams its bank robberies, with John C. Reilly as the veteran FBI agent on the digital trail, and Zo&euml; Kravitz, Pete Davidson and Anna Sawai in the cast; it runs 122 minutes and is rated R. The critics' count stands at 31 to 33 percent across the weekend's tallies—the lowest mark of Leitch's career, in more than one account—under a consensus that calls it frenetic entertainment whose ideas never cohere into a satisfying message; the A.V. Club, at C+, found two or three movies smashed together, and Time Out, at three of five, found a fun, throwaway action-thriller. Verified audiences scored it 77 to 80 percent in the same counts, a gap of more than 45 points, with a B-minus CinemaScore between the two. The desk has not seen either film; it files the week's cinema record as two splits of different shapes—one film divided against itself at its centre, one divided between the people who review films and the people who bought tickets.

Worth Watching — The History of Concrete

The desk has not screened this film. The publisher has, and the publisher is the source of this item; it stands here on his tip, treated by the house method. The History of Concrete is John Wilson's documentary feature—his directorial debut in the form, after his HBO series How To with John Wilson—premiered at Sundance on January 22, 2026 and released by Magnolia Pictures on September 18, 2026, at 100 minutes in the reviews' count. It was reviewed by the New York Times, Time, and IndieWire, among others. The record the reviews converge on is this: a deadpan inquiry into concrete—its Roman endurance, its American crumbling, the oldest concrete street in the country at Bellefontaine, Ohio, a Brooklyn-Queens Expressway described to Wilson as a ticking time bomb—turns, in its final movement, into a portrait of Jack Macco, a Long Island rock musician Wilson meets handing out liquor samples, and of Macco's late fianc&eacute;e Dorothy Chin Brandt, the first female Asian American judge in New York State, who died on January 27, 2025, at 78. On the film around that turn, the file agrees in its parts: IndieWire's David Ehrlich calls it consistently hilarious and sneakily profound, sustained by a tension between order and entropy—concrete as the material men scratch their names into as a bid for immortality, and use to build the burial vaults that hold them after. The New York Times' Alissa Wilkinson, in the praise carried with the film, records being left wondering how a movie about concrete could leave a lump in the throat; the Guardian's Adrian Horton calls it consistently laugh-out-loud funny, compelling and surprising; the New Yorker's Richard Brody finds it rich in an authentic sense of discovery, and pointedly, urgently political. RogerEbert.com's account files the reservation the favorable reviews concede in passing: the film is in substance a long episode of the HBO series, and the history of its title takes up only a small portion of its running time—and a college review filed November 13 files the cooler edge, a narration and a comic persona that reviewer found an acquired taste. The film took the Best Narration prize at the Critics Choice Documentary Awards, in the November 14 account filed below. The peg on this paper is plain: Friday's Special Report, Concrete: What the Record Shows About the Most Consumed Material on Earth (November 13), covers the material; this item covers the film.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, Scrooge's score: Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol stands at 51 percent from 59 reviews in its opening count, 50 percent from 70 in a second, 51 percent from 111 in the Friday weekend guide, and 53 percent from 116 in the count taken November 14, with Metacritic at 46 in one listing and 47 in another—a film whose measure moves because the review file is still arriving, printed here as a moving measure. Ehrlich's IndieWire grade likewise stands at C-minus in one roundup and C-plus in another; the desk prints both and adopts neither. Second, the Empress's war: Collider places Franz at the front lines of the Sardinian War, while the British reports describe his return from a war against Napoleon, and from conflict with Napoleon; the desk prints the attributions as filed. Third, the book's count: The Times calls No Such Thing As Monday Hughes's second novel, and the Chicago Review of Books calls it her third book; Hughes's bibliography carries a poetry collection ahead of the novels, and the desk prints both counts as their papers filed them. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts are single-valued: No Such Thing As Monday was published in the United States on November 10, 2026, by Henry Holt, at 224 pages and $26.99, and stands first in the week's fiction tally; the third and final season of The Empress was released on Netflix on November 12; Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol and How to Rob a Bank both opened on November 13; and The History of Concrete premiered at Sundance on January 22, 2026, and was released by Magnolia Pictures on September 18, 2026. The desk has not read the book and has not watched the screen works. The log proceeds to Sunday's watches.

 The Clippings Filed With This Feature

 Everything the desk read for the feature above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk's feature is the only item in this file stamped objective. 19 items.

 
 SubjectiveBook Marks — the best reviewed books of the week, November 13, 2026Book Marks tallies the week's reviews and ranks No Such Thing As Monday by Siân Hughes first in fiction with five rave reviews, two positive and one mixed; Xita Rubert's The Key Biscayne Affair follows at three rave and two positive, and Annie Proulx Stories stands third at four rave. In nonfiction, James Gleick's The Telephone stands first at four rave and three positive, ahead of Nick Paumgarten's The Intangibles at five rave and one positive; Lauren Elkin's Vocal Break and Nancy Isenberg's Aristocracy, American Style share third, and Mona Chalabi's Ten Lives closes the list. The tally quotes Leah Greenblatt of the New York Times on Hughes, Alexandra Jacobs of the New York Times on Gleick, and Fiona Sturges of the Guardian on Elkin.

 SubjectiveLiterary Hub — five book reviews you need to read this week, November 12, 2026The week's selected quintet: Hillary Kelly in The Atlantic on M. John Harrison's The End of Everything, Merve Emre in The New Yorker on Tom Overton's John Berger, Ed Park on Cleo Birdwell's Amazons, Ryan Ruby in Bookforum on Emily Ogden's Darkness Becomes Bright, and Josef Burton on Akbar Shahid Ahmed's Crossing the Red Line. No review of the week's tally-leading novel stands among the five.

 SubjectiveChicago Review of Books — No Such Thing As Monday is a photo album of one woman's trauma and triumphsThe Chicago review, published November 11, takes Hughes's book—which it calls her third—as the lifetime of Stephanie, called Steffie: childhood to middle age against the background of England, carrying abandonment, familial guilt, favoritism and poverty. Steffie is hard-headed and hilarious, compelling, not always likeable and never unlikeable; the novel unveils itself slowly and with intention, its chapter titles foreshadowing what comes, each chapter a set of pages in a photo album that feels complete by the end. The review lists the book from Henry Holt and Company, published November 10, 2026.

 SubjectiveThe Times — a gritty modern black comedy inspired by a medieval poemThe Times review of what it calls Hughes's tragicomic second novel: Steffie, a woman working in a dry cleaner's, cannot escape the taint of her past; the novel opens as she finds her father Stan dead in his chair. Humour is how Steffie copes, and how the reader copes with a harrowing tale of penury and hurt; as the book dives into her violent childhood in the 1970s and 1980s in the West Midlands, the dark comedy recedes, and Hughes could have gone further and funnier. Where she excels is in meandering through the slippages of memory. The title derives from Steffie's account of manipulation and her estrangement from her sister Caroline, and the book's extended metaphor of dirty laundry comes from the medieval poem called Purity or Cleanness. The verdict: a decent follow-up to Pearl, positioning itself as the lesser work.

 SubjectiveKirkus Reviews — No Such Thing As MondayKirkus, in the notice posted September 14, 2026, records the book's facts—Henry Holt, publication November 10, 2026, 224 pages, ISBN 9781250459572—and its verdict in one line: with an alchemy like Douglas Stuart's, Hughes transforms the dross of Steffie's life into literary gold.

 SubjectiveShelf Awareness — review of No Such Thing As Monday, August 28, 2026Shelf Awareness lists the book at $26.99 in hardcover, 224 pages, ISBN 9781250459572, from Holt, November 10, 2026, and reviews it as a poignant, darkly satirical story inspired by a medieval poem called Cleanness: Steffie Cartwright, who expertly removes laundry stains at the dry cleaner's where she works, cannot erase the memories of her blemished past; she grew up near Birmingham under a violent bully of a father who ran dogfights at the local pub, and with Stan dead she reckons with shame and guilt over her sister Caroline, who ran away in her teens.

 SubjectiveMacmillan — No Such Thing as Monday, the publisher's recordThe publisher's page records the book as a novel by Siân Hughes, Henry Holt and Company, on sale November 10, 2026, 224 pages, ISBN 9781250459572, and describes it in its own copy: from a Booker Prize-longlisted author, a woman tries to overcome her abusive past and find her estranged sister, in a deeply moving and darkly humorous quest for redemption, written in the working-class British realist tradition of Douglas Stuart and Andrea Arnold.

 SubjectiveCollider — The Empress delivers a satisfying ending for one of Netflix's best hidden gemsCollider's review, published November 12, takes the German period drama as one of Netflix's most underrated gems: the third and final season turns darker and more tense, opening months after Franz left to command his army on the front lines of the Sardinian War. Its ending fudges history in the name of love, glossing the harrowing events of Elisabeth's later life and turning the establishment of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy into a fresh start for Franz and Elisabeth; not truthful, the review holds, and a satisfying, poignant conclusion all the same, with the chemistry of its leads grounding the geopolitics and the Andrássy relationship rushed.

 SubjectiveMidgard Times — The Empress season 3: a rushed finale that turns history into bullet pointsThe Midgard Times review, published November 13 and scored 3.5 of 10, holds that the third and final season never allows any moment, scene, feeling or action to linger, speedrunning its material until investment fails; that the serial peaked in a first season that was not all that good; and that its creator's one guiding instinct in the final season was to wrap everything up because no fourth season follows. It records Franz returning from the war a changed, cold and distant man, and Maximilian becoming Mexico's ruler.

 SubjectiveAbsolute Geeks — The Empress season 3: Netflix's hidden gem finally gets its happy endingAbsolute Geeks scores the final season four of five: a darker, politically charged farewell anchored by superb chemistry and gorgeous production design, with Gabriela Reumer's costumes among the best work in streaming period drama, and Devrim Lingnau Islamoğlu radiant as an empress tasting freedom. A rushed Hungarian subplot and loose history hold it back; the finale is more fairytale than biography, sidestepping the tragedy of her son Rudolf and handling her assassination as onscreen text, and as the ending of the story the serial has told, it is bittersweet, earned and genuinely lovely.

 SubjectiveScreenRant — The Empress: hands down Netflix's best historical dramaScreenRant's November 14 account calls the German original a beautiful, intriguing series in the line of The Crown and Bridgerton, with no bad season: the first installment earned an 85 percent audience score and the second a nearly perfect 92 percent, and the third and final season, now streaming, it calls a true masterpiece, its empress grown and weary and doing what she does best—whatever she wants—with something to say about mental health, women's rights and autonomy.

 SubjectiveRotten Tomatoes — Ebenezer (2026)The Rotten Tomatoes page for Ebenezer records the film's facts—director Ti West, screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern, distributor Paramount Pictures, rated PG-13 for frightening material, released in theaters November 13, 2026—and its consensus: decking its halls with evocative production design while Johnny Depp is filled with the bah-humbug spirit, Ebenezer does not scrooge Dickens's classic tale up, and plays things too safe to stand out among its long line of remakes. The page carries a three-of-four review holding that Depp is terrific as Scrooge and that West brings the right amount of creep factor to the holiday classic.

 SubjectiveCBR — Johnny Depp's new dark fantasy film is already very polarizingCBR, published November 12, records the film at 50 percent on Rotten Tomatoes on its opening—as many critics praising it as calling it bad. It files Andrea Chase of Killer Movie Reviews, for whom West lets the audience experience the story as if for the first time, evoking the horror Dickens intended, and Louisa Moore of Screen Zealots, for whom West gives the tale a spooky, terrifying makeover without losing its heart; against them, Elliott Collins of Movie Files, for whom the horror never goes far enough, Depp's eccentricity adds little, and the redemption feels unearned, and CBR's own Chris La Vigna at five of ten, for whom it falls flat in the end.

 SubjectiveWeekend guide, November 13 to 15, 2026 — Ebenezer's reviews are in, and they're splitA weekend viewing guide verified November 13 records Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol at 51 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 111 reviews, its number still moving, with audiences happier in early exit polls at about four and a half stars; the film took $1.5 million in Thursday previews and was expected to open at about $20 million, enough for first place. The same guide records How to Rob a Bank, David Leitch's heist comedy with Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz and Pete Davidson, at 31 percent from 77 reviews, off $900,000 in previews and headed for a single-digit-millions weekend.

 SubjectiveMovieWeb — How to Rob a Bank scores big with audiences on Rotten TomatoesMovieWeb, published November 14, records How to Rob a Bank at 33 percent from the critics—the worst Tomatometer score of David Leitch's career—against an 80 percent Popcornmeter from verified audiences averaging four of five stars, a gap of 47 points; its consensus calls the film frenetic entertainment with a lot on its mind that cannot make its ideas cohere. The film, 122 minutes and rated R, follows Nicholas Hoult's Pittsburgh crew livestreaming its robberies while John C. Reilly's FBI agent and Zoë Kravitz's software engineer work the digital trail; it took $900,000 in previews, carries a B-minus CinemaScore, and is projected toward a modest opening on a reported budget of $40 to $60 million.

 SubjectiveIndieWire, via Letterboxd — David Ehrlich on The History of ConcreteDavid Ehrlich's review, published on Letterboxd January 23, 2026 and continuing on IndieWire, records what John Wilson thinks about when he thinks about concrete: DMX, Hallmark movies, Kim Kardashian, a trailblazing Asian American judge, the world's first 3D-printed Starbucks, and a 3,100-mile footrace honoring a dead Brooklyn cult leader. He calls Wilson a sweetly Dantean scavenger who collages a broken existence back together from first-person video snippets and unpredictable detours, and the film consistently hilarious and sneakily profound, sustained by an internal tension between order and entropy across its 100 minutes—its making and its funding folded into the material itself.

 SubjectiveRogerEbert.com — The History of Concrete: John Wilson stuns with rock-solid comic observationsThe RogerEbert.com review, published September 18, 2026, takes Wilson's feature as in substance a long episode of his HBO series, with proportionately more of his personality and private life: the history of concrete of its title takes up only a small portion of the movie, the first twelve minutes recap the director's life after his show ended, and the film leaps from his personal life to those of his interview subjects, friends and acquaintances in the Wikipedia rabbit-hole manner of the series.

 SubjectiveIn Review Online — The History of Concrete, John WilsonIn Review Online, in the review republished September 18, records the film's facts—director John Wilson, distributor Magnolia Pictures, in theaters September 18, running time one hour 41 minutes—and its reading: Wilson, at a creative and psychic standstill after his series ended in 2023, dives down multiple simultaneous rabbit holes, from a Hallmark movie studio to urban gentrification to the rapper DMX, and finds in Jack, a liquor sales rep fronting a struggling rock band, a late tragedy that throws the whole relationship into relief. For Wilson, in this account, concrete is the ultimate binder and a manifestation of entropy and impermanence, and the film is a tremendous ode to hope and kindness in the face of inevitable collapse.

 SubjectiveVancouver International Film Festival — The History of Concrete, with the praise filed with the filmThe festival page for the film describes Wilson applying the best practices of a Hallmark pitching workshop to his documentary about concrete, and assembling low-resolution vérité vignettes into collages that complement his deadpan philosophising. It carries the praise filed with the film: Richard Brody of the New Yorker, for whom concrete turns out remarkably, pointedly, urgently political, and the film rich in an authentic sense of discovery; Adrian Horton of the Guardian, consistently laugh-out-loud funny, compelling and surprising; and Alissa Wilkinson of the New York Times, left wondering how a movie about concrete could leave a lump in the throat.
